elements.text: A personal take from someone who's spent years keeping enterprise systems alive — on the number that changes everything.
In enterprise software, most of the work isn't building new things. It's keeping old things running. So when I found a number about exactly that problem, I couldn't stop thinking about it.

"AI writes code now, so there's less work for developers." I hear this constantly.

It assumes the total amount of work is fixed and AI just does the same work faster, with fewer people. After years inside large engineering orgs, I don't think that's how it plays out.

Globally, there's an estimated 800 billion lines of legacy code in production. Modernizing it has historically cost ~$10-15 per line — too expensive for most of it to ever get touched.

With AI handling analysis, refactoring, and testing, that's dropping toward ~$2 per line. The gap: an addressable opportunity north of $1.6 trillion.

Every org has one. The original team is gone, the docs are thin, and every change request gets pushed to "next quarter" because the risk-to-reward isn't there.

That system isn't an edge case — it's where a huge share of an engineering org's time, budget, and stress actually goes.

elements.text: The engineers who spent years on legacy systems — the ones everyone avoided — suddenly have the skill set that matters most.
What This Means For The Industry

If AI drops modernization cost by 5-10x, the naive read is: same work, less money.

But I think the opposite happens — a huge backlog of "someday, maybe" projects suddenly clears the bar. The market doesn't shrink. It widens, because the threshold for "worth doing" just dropped.

I don't have this all figured out. But after years watching legacy systems pile up while everyone chased the next shiny feature, this is the shift I've been waiting for.

I want to work through it in public — what applying AI to a real legacy system actually looks like, what breaks, what saves time, and what's still hype.
The threshold for "worth doing" just dropped — and that changes everything about where the work goes next.
A system everyone's afraid to touch. A modernization project that never got the green light. Or you're already experimenting with AI on legacy code.
Tell me about it in the comments — and follow along on LinkedIn, X, and Instagram. Let's figure this out together.
